items.followUp: Describe the structure and functions of the cell wall, with a labelled diagram.

rubric.why: Award marks for describing the membrane’s main structural components and arrangement.
rubric.description: Structure: a thin, flexible phospholipid bilayer with proteins embedded in it.
rubric.how: 1 mark for the bilayer; 1 mark for embedded proteins or the fluid-mosaic arrangement, including the hydrophilic heads and hydrophobic tails if described instead of the model answer’s wording.

rubric.why: Selective permeability is a key function of the cell membrane.
rubric.description: Function: controls the movement of substances into and out of the cell.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that the membrane regulates entry and exit of substances.

rubric.why: A labelled diagram should show the bilayer’s orientation and a membrane protein.
rubric.description: Diagram: show and label the two layers, outward-facing heads, inward-facing tails and a membrane protein.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a recognisable, labelled bilayer showing the heads and tails in the correct orientation and at least one protein.

modelAnswer: The cell membrane is a thin, flexible boundary that surrounds the cytoplasm and separates it from the external environment.
It consists mainly of a phospholipid bilayer with proteins embedded in it; the hydrophilic heads face the watery environments while the hydrophobic tails face inward.
It is selectively permeable and controls the movement of substances into and out of the cell.

Diagram construction: draw two parallel rows of phospholipids; show the round heads facing outward and the tails facing inward; add an embedded protein; label the phospholipid bilayer, hydrophilic heads, hydrophobic tails and protein. No scale is required.

items.followUp: Define classification and write the taxonomic hierarchy from kingdom to order, describing each level.

rubric.why: The definition must convey that classification uses ordered levels or categories.
rubric.description: Define taxonomic hierarchy as the arrangement of organisms into successive classification levels.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing ordered taxonomic categories or levels.

rubric.why: The ranks must be stated in the correct order from the broadest level requested.
rubric.description: List the hierarchy in order: kingdom, phylum, class, order, family.
rubric.how: Award 2 marks for the correct sequence; award 1 mark if there is one omission or a minor order error.

rubric.why: Descriptions show how groups at successive ranks are formed.
rubric.description: Describe the ranks: a kingdom contains phyla; a phylum contains classes; a class contains orders; an order contains families; a family contains related genera.
rubric.how: Award 2 marks for accurate descriptions of the grouping relationships, allowing equivalent wording.

modelAnswer: A taxonomic hierarchy is the arrangement of organisms into successive, ranked groups called taxa, from broad groups to increasingly specific ones.
Kingdom is the broadest rank and contains related phyla.
A phylum contains related classes.
A class contains related orders.
An order contains related families.
A family contains related genera.

items.followUp: Describe the light-independent reactions of photosynthesis and state where they occur.

rubric.why: The light reaction takes place on the thylakoid membranes of chloroplasts.
rubric.description: State the site of the light reaction.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for thylakoids or grana of the chloroplast.

rubric.why: Absorption of light by chlorophyll initiates the reaction.
rubric.description: Explain that chlorophyll absorbs light energy.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking chlorophyll with absorption of light.

rubric.why: Splitting water supplies electrons and releases oxygen.
rubric.description: Describe photolysis of water and the release of oxygen.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for water splitting and oxygen production.

rubric.why: ATP and NADPH are the energy-rich products used in the next stage of photosynthesis.
rubric.description: State that ATP and NADPH are produced.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for both ATP and NADPH, or equivalent accurate descriptions of their formation.

modelAnswer: The light reaction occurs on the thylakoid membranes in the grana of chloroplasts.
Chlorophyll absorbs light energy, exciting electrons to a higher energy level.
Light energy splits water molecules by photolysis; oxygen is released, and hydrogen ions and electrons are produced.
The excited electrons pass through an electron transport chain, and their energy is used to make ATP by photophosphorylation.
Hydrogen and electrons reduce NADP to NADPH; ATP and NADPH are used in the light-independent reaction.

items.followUp: Explain the causes and symptoms of diarrhoea and constipation, and state how each can be managed.

rubric.why: Diarrhoea is a common gut disorder and its defining feature is frequent loose or watery stools.
rubric.description: Describe diarrhoea and its principal effect.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for frequent loose or watery stools and 1 mark for explaining that it can cause loss of water and salts or dehydration.

rubric.why: Constipation involves difficult passage of hard stools.
rubric.description: Describe constipation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for hard, dry stools or difficulty in passing stools.

rubric.why: An ulcer is a disorder involving damage to the lining of the gut.
rubric.description: Describe peptic ulcer as a sore or erosion in the stomach or intestinal lining.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying an ulcer as damage or a sore in the gut lining.

rubric.why: Appendicitis is an inflammatory disorder of a gut-associated structure.
rubric.description: Describe appendicitis as inflammation of the appendix, commonly associated with abdominal pain.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying inflammation of the appendix.

modelAnswer: Diarrhoea is the frequent passage of loose, watery stools. It causes excessive loss of water and salts and may lead to dehydration.
Constipation is the difficult passage of hard, dry stools, often due to slow movement of faeces through the large intestine.
A peptic ulcer is a sore or erosion in the lining of the stomach or intestine; it may cause pain and bleeding.
Appendicitis is inflammation of the appendix and commonly causes abdominal pain.

items.followUp: Define guttation and explain how humidity, temperature and wind affect transpiration.

rubric.why: The definition should identify water-vapour loss from above-ground plant parts.
rubric.description: Define transpiration.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for loss of water vapour from the aerial parts of a plant, especially leaves.

rubric.why: Higher temperature generally increases evaporation and transpiration.
rubric.description: State the effect of temperature.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that higher temperature generally increases the rate.

rubric.why: Humid air reduces the water-vapour gradient between the leaf and the air.
rubric.description: State the effect of humidity.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that higher humidity decreases the rate.

rubric.why: Moving air removes moist air around the leaf and can increase water loss.
rubric.description: State the effect of wind or air movement.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that wind generally increases the rate by removing moist air around leaves.

modelAnswer: Transpiration is the loss of water vapour from the aerial parts of a plant, mainly through the stomata of leaves.
Higher temperature generally increases the rate of transpiration by increasing evaporation.
High humidity decreases the rate because the difference in water-vapour concentration between the leaf and air is smaller.
Wind generally increases the rate by carrying away moist air around the leaves.

items.followUp: Define genetics and state what it studies.

rubric.why: The definition should identify cell biology as the study of cells and their characteristics.
rubric.description: Define cell biology.
rubric.how: Award 2 marks for stating that it is the study of cells; award 1 mark if the answer only says it studies cell structure or cell function.

modelAnswer: Cell biology is the branch of biology that studies cells, including their structure and functions.

items.followUp: Define an organ and give one example from a plant or animal.

rubric.why: A tissue is a group of cells working together to perform a particular function.
rubric.description: Define tissue.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing a tissue as a group of cells working together for a function.

rubric.why: A valid example demonstrates understanding of the term.
rubric.description: Give an example of a tissue.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct tissue example, such as muscle tissue or xylem.

modelAnswer: A tissue is a group of similar cells working together to perform a specific function.
Muscle tissue is an example.

items.followUp: What is tissue organisation? Give one example showing how tissues form an organ.

rubric.why: Cellular organisation refers to the arrangement of cells into progressively higher levels of organisation.
rubric.description: Explain the levels of cellular organisation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for showing that cells form tissues and tissues form organs, with organ systems also acceptable.

rubric.why: A suitable example should show cells organised into a higher-level structure.
rubric.description: Give an example of cellular organisation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a valid example showing cells forming a tissue or an organ, such as muscle cells forming muscle tissue in the heart.

modelAnswer: Cellular organisation is the arrangement of cells into tissues, tissues into organs, and organs into organ systems.
For example, muscle cells form muscle tissue, which is part of the heart.
